questions.title: Why ServiceNow Is a Platform, Not Just an ITSM Tool
questions.prompt: Your manager introduces ServiceNow to a new hire as 'our ITSM ticketing tool.' What's incomplete about that description, and what fact about the incident table itself best explains why?
questions.modelAnswer: ServiceNow's underlying product is the Now Platform, and ITSM (Incident, Problem, Change, Request) is just one application built on top of it, alongside ITOM, HR Service Delivery, Customer Service Management, Security Operations, and thousands of custom scoped applications. The fact that makes this concrete rather than semantic: the incident table is an ordinary database table, its form is built with the same Form Designer any custom app uses, and the logic that auto-assigns an incident runs on the exact same Business Rule and Client Script engine available to any other application on the instance. Nothing about incident is architecturally special. That's why the skills this path teaches -- tables, forms, scripting, security -- are platform skills, not ITSM skills, and transfer to any application running on the same instance.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd gently correct the framing: ITSM is the product most people meet first, but it's one tenant on the Now Platform, not the platform itself. The tell is that incident is just a table like any other -- same form engine, same Business Rule and Client Script mechanism any custom app uses. So when I describe my own skill set, I say 'ServiceNow platform skills, first applied through ITSM' rather than 'ITSM skills,' because that's literally how job postings read too -- 'ServiceNow Administrator,' not 'ITSM Administrator.'
commonMistakes: Treating the incident table as architecturally different from a custom app's tables
Assuming admin/dev skills learned on ITSM don't transfer to HR Service Delivery, CSM, or custom apps
Naming only ITSM when asked what ServiceNow 'does', missing ITOM, HRSD, CSM, SecOps
Confusing 'the oldest, most common product' with 'the whole platform'
keyPoints: Now Platform is the underlying product; ITSM is one application on it
Incident's table, form, and scripting mechanism are identical to any custom app's
Other products on the same platform: ITOM, HRSD, CSM, SecOps, custom scoped apps
This is why the market treats ServiceNow skills as transferable across whichever app an employer runs

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the Now Platform vs. ITSM-application distinction
Names at least two other real products built on the same platform
Explains why the incident table isn't architecturally special

questions.title: The Four Layers of the Now Platform
questions.prompt: Name the four layers of the Now Platform architecture model, and explain why ACLs, Flow Designer, and integration are described as cutting across all of them rather than belonging to just one layer.
questions.modelAnswer: The four layers are: the database layer (the Glide Data Model -- tables, fields, table extension, with no behavior of its own), the application layer (forms, lists, and the logic that drives them -- Business Rules, Client Scripts, Script Includes), the UI layer (how all of that renders to a screen, whether Classic UI/UI16 or the newer Next Experience/Workspaces), and platform services that cut across every layer at once -- ACLs, Flow Designer/workflow, and integration (REST APIs, IntegrationHub). Those three are cross-cutting rather than belonging to one layer because each of them reaches into the database, application, and UI layers simultaneously: an ACL governs a database-layer table or field, is enforced no matter which UI layer renders the request, and applies whether the request came through a form or an API call. The same is true of Flow Designer (spans tables, approvals, and UI) and integration (moves data in and out across all three layers at once).
questions.professionalAnswer: I think of it as three stacked layers plus one thing that isn't really a layer at all. Database at the bottom (Glide Data Model), application in the middle (forms, lists, Business Rules, Client Scripts), UI on top (Classic UI/UI16 or Next Experience). ACLs, Flow Designer, and integration don't sit in that stack -- they reach through all three at once. An ACL on a table doesn't care if you're hitting it through Classic UI, a Workspace, or the Table API; it's enforced identically everywhere, which is exactly why it's cross-cutting instead of belonging to any single layer.
commonMistakes: Listing only two or three layers instead of all four
Placing ACLs or Flow Designer inside one layer instead of recognizing them as cross-cutting
Treating Classic UI and Next Experience as different platforms instead of two UI-layer presentation choices over the same data
Confusing the UI layer with the application layer (forms/lists are application-layer; how they render is UI-layer)
keyPoints: Database layer = Glide Data Model: tables, fields, table extension, no behavior
Application layer = forms, lists, Business Rules, Client Scripts, Script Includes
UI layer = Classic UI/UI16 and Next Experience/Workspaces, rendering the same underlying data
ACLs, Flow Designer, and integration are cross-cutting platform services, not a fourth stacked layer

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly names all four layers/categories
Correctly explains why ACLs/Flow Designer/integration are cross-cutting
Clarity and use of correct terminology

questions.title: Why a Report Against the Task Table Mixes Incidents, Problems, and Changes
questions.prompt: A colleague builds a report directly against the `task` table expecting to see only generic task records, but it returns incidents, problems, and change requests all mixed together. Why does that happen, and is it a bug?
questions.modelAnswer: It's not a bug -- it's exactly how table extension is supposed to work. `task` is a base table, deliberately generic, and `incident`, `problem`, and `change_request` all extend it, meaning each one inherits every field `task` has (short_description, state, priority, assignment_group, and more) and adds its own fields on top (incident adds caller_id and category, for example). Because an extended table's record is also technically a row that satisfies a query against its parent, any report or list built directly against `task` with no further filtering returns every record from every table that extends it -- incidents, problems, changes, and request items -- all mixed together, because each one genuinely *is* a task underneath its extra fields. This is exactly the mechanism that lets a manager build one 'all open work across every queue' dashboard without separately querying four tables and merging the results by hand.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell them it's working as designed, not broken. `incident`, `problem`, and `change_request` all extend `task`, so every incident row is also, technically, a task row. Query `task` with no filter and you get all of them back together, because that's literally what table extension means -- shared fields defined once on the parent, inherited everywhere. If they only wanted incidents, the fix is adding a filter on `sys_class_name`, not treating the mixed result as a defect.
commonMistakes: Assuming a query against a base table should somehow know to exclude extended-table records
Not realizing `incident`, `problem`, and `change_request` all extend the same `task` table
Thinking table extension is a naming convention rather than real inheritance
Missing that this is the same mechanism that lets 'all open work' dashboards exist across queues
keyPoints: `task` is a deliberately generic base table that incident, problem, and change_request all extend
Table extension is real inheritance: the child gets every parent field plus its own
An extended-table record satisfies a query against its parent table too
This is intended behavior, not a bug -- it's what powers cross-queue 'all open work' reporting

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies table extension as the cause
Explains that an extended record also satisfies the parent-table query
Correctly states this is intended behavior, not a bug

questions.title: What's Actually Stored in a Reference Field
questions.prompt: An Incident's `caller_id` field displays 'Fred Luddy.' What value is actually stored in that column, and why does the displayed name update automatically if Fred's name is edited in his user record?
questions.modelAnswer: The column stores the `sys_id` of the referenced `sys_user` record, not the text 'Fred Luddy.' A reference field is ServiceNow's equivalent of a relational foreign key: it holds a pointer to a specific row on another table. What the form shows is a live lookup of that referenced record's display value, performed every time the form renders -- it isn't text sitting in `caller_id` itself. So if Fred's name is changed in `sys_user`, every incident that references him shows the new name immediately, because nothing about the stored reference (the sys_id) changed; only the record being pointed at was edited.
questions.professionalAnswer: What's stored is the sys_id of the sys_user record, full stop -- the name you see is just a live display-value lookup against whatever that sys_id currently points to. That's exactly why renaming a user in sys_user instantly updates every incident, change, and request that references them: the pointer never moved, only the thing it points at changed. I use this constantly when I'm debugging a 'wrong name showing' issue -- I check whether the reference itself is wrong (wrong sys_id) versus the referenced record's data being wrong, because those are two completely different fixes.
commonMistakes: Assuming the field stores the display text ('Fred Luddy') rather than the sys_id
Thinking the displayed name is a one-time copy rather than a live lookup
Confusing a reference field's auto-complete/preview-icon behavior with plain free text
Not recognizing related lists as the reverse direction of the same reference relationship
keyPoints: A reference field stores the referenced record's sys_id, not its display text
The displayed value is a live lookup against the referenced record each time the form renders
Editing the referenced record updates every field that points to it, automatically
This is ServiceNow's version of a relational foreign key

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies that the sys_id, not the display text, is stored
Correctly explains why the display updates automatically
Uses correct terminology (reference field, display value)

questions.title: Why Adding a New ACL Can Break Access That Used to Work
questions.prompt: An admin adds a new, narrower ACL to tighten security on a table. Afterward, several users who used to have read access start getting denied, even though nothing about the ACLs they already matched changed. Why?
questions.modelAnswer: Every access rule in ServiceNow lives on `sys_security_acl`, and when more than one ACL applies to the same operation on the same record or field, every single applicable ACL must pass -- it's an AND across all of them, never an OR. Adding a new ACL never removes anything that already existed; it just adds one more rule that now also has to pass for access to be granted. If a user already satisfied every prior ACL but fails this new, narrower one, the whole operation is denied, even though none of the ACLs that used to let them in were touched. This is exactly the mistake new admins make: they assume access is granted if a user matches *any* passing ACL, when the real rule is that *all* applicable ACLs must pass, so one new failing rule is enough to take away access that previously worked.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is the single most common 'but I didn't change anything!' ticket an admin files against themselves. ACLs AND together, they don't OR -- so a brand-new ACL doesn't replace or compete with the old ones, it just adds one more condition to the chain. If the new ACL is narrower than what those users actually have, it's now the weak link, and one failing link in an AND chain denies the whole thing. My first question whenever 'access that used to work' breaks right after an ACL change is always: what's the newest ACL on this table, and does everyone affected actually satisfy it?
commonMistakes: Assuming ACLs combine with OR, so matching any one grants access
Believing a new ACL can only add access, never remove it
Not checking the most recently added ACL first when 'access that used to work' suddenly fails
Confusing table-level ACL changes with field-level ACL changes when troubleshooting
keyPoints: Every ACL lives on `sys_security_acl`
All applicable ACLs must pass (AND), not just one (OR)
A new, narrower ACL adds one more condition to an existing AND chain -- it can revoke access without touching prior rules
The first troubleshooting step after an access regression is checking the newest ACL change

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies AND (not OR) evaluation across applicable ACLs
Explains why a new ACL can break access without modifying existing ACLs
References `sys_security_acl` or equivalent correct terminology

questions.title: A User Can Read the Incident but Not One Field — Why?
questions.prompt: A user has full read access to Incident records and can open any incident just fine, but one specific field (say, a confidential legal-hold note) never shows up for them no matter which incident they open. How is that possible, and which two kinds of ACL are involved?
questions.modelAnswer: Two separate ACLs are involved: a table-level ACL (`incident.read`) that governs whether the user can access the record at all, and a field-level ACL that governs visibility of that one specific field. Passing the table-level check is necessary but not sufficient -- for any field the user is trying to read, the platform also checks whether a field-level ACL exists for that specific field, and if one does, it must pass too, in addition to (never instead of) the table-level ACL. This user clearly passes `incident.read`, which is why the record opens at all, but a field-level ACL scoped to the legal-hold note is blocking that one field regardless of the record. Table-level and field-level ACLs stack; a user can pass one and fail the other.
questions.professionalAnswer: That's the table-level versus field-level distinction working exactly as designed. They pass `incident.read`, that's a table-level check, that's why the record opens. But a field-level ACL is a completely separate rule attached to that one field, and it's evaluated *in addition to* the table-level ACL, not as a substitute for it. So they can clear the record-wide check and still get blocked on one specific field, every single time, because that field has its own gatekeeper. If I needed to confirm this, I'd go straight to the Access Control list filtered to `incident` and that field's name.
commonMistakes: Assuming one ACL passing means the whole record (including every field) is visible
Not realizing field-level ACLs are checked in addition to, not instead of, table-level ACLs
Thinking a field-level restriction implies the record-level ACL is misconfigured
Confusing a hidden field (UI Policy) with a field the ACL layer is actually blocking
keyPoints: Table-level ACL (e.g. `incident.read`) governs whether the user can access the record at all
Field-level ACL governs visibility/write access to one specific field
Field-level ACLs are checked in addition to the table-level ACL, never as a replacement
Passing the table-level check is necessary but not sufficient for seeing every field

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes table-level from field-level ACLs
Correctly explains that both must pass, stacking rather than substituting
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: What Actually Runs When You Click Save on an Incident
questions.prompt: Explain what a Business Rule actually is in ServiceNow terms, which table every Business Rule lives on, and why it's considered more powerful -- and more dangerous -- than a UI Policy.
questions.modelAnswer: A Business Rule is a server-side script attached to a table, stored as a row on `sys_script`, that the platform runs automatically when a record on that table is inserted, updated, deleted, or queried -- no user ever clicks a button to trigger it. It runs on the ServiceNow application server, inside the same transaction as the database write, with full GlideRecord access to any table, not just the one the user is looking at: a Business Rule on Incident can query sys_user, update change_request, or write to an unrelated custom table, all before or after the save finishes. That server-side reach is exactly why it's more powerful than a UI Policy, which can only hide or require a field in the browser. It's also more dangerous for the same reason: because it runs on every matching database operation with no sandboxing, a careless Business Rule doesn't just produce one wrong answer on one form, it can run thousands of times a day on every record of that type, with access the logged-in user might not even have themselves.
questions.professionalAnswer: A Business Rule is server-side logic on `sys_script` that fires automatically on insert, update, delete, or query -- nobody clicks 'run,' it just happens as part of the save. Because it runs on the server with full GlideRecord access, it can touch any table, not just the one in front of the user, which is a different order of power than a UI Policy that can only hide a field in someone's browser. That power cuts both ways -- it's exactly why I treat every Business Rule I write as production code the moment I activate it, because it runs with system-level reach on every single matching save, whether I tested that specific edge case or not.
commonMistakes: Thinking Business Rules run in the browser like Client Scripts
Not realizing a Business Rule can query or write to tables other than the one it's attached to
Underestimating how 'full database access, no sandboxing' makes a careless rule dangerous at scale
Confusing a Business Rule's power with a UI Policy's, which can only affect field state in the browser
keyPoints: Business Rule = server-side script on `sys_script`, runs on insert/update/delete/query automatically
Runs on the application server with full GlideRecord access to any table
More powerful than a UI Policy, which can only hide/require a field client-side
More dangerous because it runs with system-level reach on every matching database operation

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines a Business Rule and names `sys_script`
Correctly explains server-side execution and cross-table reach
Correctly contrasts power/danger versus a UI Policy

questions.title: Choosing the Right Business Rule Timing
questions.prompt: You need a rule that defaults Urgency based on Priority before the record is ever saved, and a separate rule that posts a Slack notification after an Incident update without making the user wait for Slack to respond. What Business Rule timings fit each requirement, and why?
questions.modelAnswer: Defaulting Urgency from Priority belongs in a Before Business Rule: Before rules run before the record is actually written to the database, so a script that sets `current.urgency` there changes the value that gets saved, in the same transaction, with no extra database write needed. The Slack notification belongs in an Async (After) Business Rule, specifically run asynchronously: an Async rule runs after the record save completes, in a separate background process, so the user who saved the Incident doesn't have to wait for the external Slack call to finish before their save returns. Using Before for the notification would make the user's save wait on Slack's response time; using plain After instead of Async would still block the saving transaction's follow-on processing on an external network call, which is exactly what Async exists to avoid.
questions.professionalAnswer: Before, for the Urgency default -- it runs in the same transaction before the write, so it changes the value instead of triggering a second save. For the Slack notification, Async, not plain After, because I don't want the person saving the Incident sitting there waiting on an external network call that has nothing to do with their save succeeding. Async hands that off to the background so the user's transaction returns immediately and the notification happens on its own schedule a moment later.
commonMistakes: Using an After rule to set a field value, which requires a second database write instead of modifying the record before it's saved
Using a synchronous After rule for an external call, making the user wait on network latency
Confusing Display Business Rules (which run on form load, not insert/update) with Before/After
Assuming Before and After are interchangeable as long as the logic is correct
keyPoints: Before Business Rules run before the write -- the right choice for setting/defaulting a field value
After Business Rules run after the write completes, in the same transaction unless marked Async
Async Business Rules run after the write, in a background process, so the user's save doesn't wait on them
External calls (notifications, webhooks) belong in Async, not synchronous Before/After

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly assigns Before to the Urgency-default requirement
Correctly assigns Async to the Slack-notification requirement
Explains why the wrong timing would cause a real problem (extra write / blocking wait)

lessonLink.label: Review: Before, After, Async & Display Business Rules

questions.title: Why an Incident Record Is Never a Configuration Item
questions.prompt: A new administrator says, 'The laptop CI is linked to this incident, so the incident is basically a CI too.' What's wrong with that statement, and how do a CI and a work record actually relate to each other?
questions.modelAnswer: An Incident is a work record -- a task-table record representing something someone is doing, like investigating an outage -- while a Configuration Item represents something that exists, like the laptop itself, independent of whatever work is currently happening to it. They are not the same kind of thing and don't become the same thing by being linked. The connection is a reference field: the Incident has a `cmdb_ci` field pointing at the specific CI it's about. The Incident is not the laptop; it *references* the laptop. Closing the Incident doesn't delete the laptop CI, and the laptop CI continues existing, with its own state and relationships, independent of this or any other incident that ever referenced it.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd correct that right away: a CI is something that exists -- infrastructure, an application, a service -- and a work record is something being done about it. They're connected by a plain reference field, `cmdb_ci` on the Incident, not by the Incident somehow becoming a CI. The test I use is simple: does this thing need its own state and relationships tracked independent of any ticket? A laptop does. The investigation of why it's broken doesn't -- that's the Incident, and it's a completely different kind of record.
commonMistakes: Treating a work record (Incident, Problem, Change) as itself a Configuration Item because they're linked
Thinking closing or deleting the work record affects the referenced CI
Confusing the `cmdb_ci` reference field with the CI being 'part of' the incident
Using 'is this expensive/has a serial number' instead of 'does its state need tracking' as the CI test
keyPoints: A CI represents something that exists; a work record represents something being done
Incident, Problem, and Change are work records (task-table), never CIs themselves
The `cmdb_ci` reference field is how a work record points at the specific CI it's about
The CI continues to exist independently of any work record that ever referenced it

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes a CI from a work record
Correctly describes the `cmdb_ci` reference-field relationship
Clarity of the correction given to the new administrator

lessonLink.label: Review: What a Configuration Item Actually Is

questions.title: Why a Well-Implemented Instance Blocks New Straight to Closed
questions.prompt: Why should a well-implemented ServiceNow instance refuse to let an Incident move directly from New to Closed, and what two fields does a Data Policy typically require before an Incident can move to Resolved?
questions.modelAnswer: Out of the box, Incident has six real states: New, In Progress, On Hold, Resolved, Closed, and Canceled. Resolved is where the resolution evidence actually lives -- it's the state that should carry a Resolution Code and Close Notes explaining what fixed the issue. If an instance allows New to jump straight to Closed, it skips Resolved entirely, which means the Incident ends up closed with no record of what fixed it, defeating the purpose of tracking resolution at all. A correctly implemented instance enforces this with a Data Policy that makes Resolution Code and Close Notes mandatory specifically when State = Resolved (not on every record in every state), so the platform refuses the state change until both are populated, guaranteeing every closed Incident has real resolution evidence behind it.
questions.professionalAnswer: Because Resolved is where the proof of the fix lives -- Resolution Code and Close Notes. If you let New skip straight to Closed, you get a closed ticket with zero record of what actually happened, and six months later nobody can explain why it's closed. The fix is a Data Policy that makes those two fields mandatory the moment State = Resolved, not mandatory everywhere, everywhere all the time -- just at that one gate, which is exactly the kind of conditional, state-driven requirement Data Policies are built for.
commonMistakes: Making Resolution Code and Close Notes mandatory on every state instead of only when State = Resolved
Not realizing New-to-Closed should be blocked at all, treating it as a minor convenience shortcut
Using a UI Policy instead of a Data Policy, which wouldn't enforce the rule against an API-created or imported record
Confusing Resolved (pending caller confirmation) with Closed (confirmed final) as if they were interchangeable
keyPoints: Incident's six states: New, In Progress, On Hold, Resolved, Closed, Canceled
Resolved is where resolution evidence (Resolution Code, Close Notes) must be recorded
A well-implemented instance blocks New straight to Closed, forcing every Incident through Resolved first
A Data Policy enforces Resolution Code and Close Notes as mandatory specifically when State = Resolved

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why New-to-Closed should be blocked
Correctly names Resolution Code and Close Notes as the required fields
Correctly identifies Data Policy as the enforcement mechanism

questions.title: Write the Canonical GlideRecord Query for Active P1 Incidents
questions.prompt: Write a server-side script that queries all active, Priority 1 Incidents and logs each one's number. Then explain what `.addQuery()` does before `.query()` runs, and what `.next()` actually returns on each loop iteration.
questions.modelAnswer: The canonical pattern: `new GlideRecord('incident')` creates the cursor, two `.addQuery()` calls add filter conditions that combine with AND by default (active AND priority 1 -- not either/or), `.query()` is the line that actually sends the built-up conditions to the database (nothing before it touches the database at all), and `while (gr.next())` walks the result set one row at a time. `.next()` does two things in one call: it advances the cursor to the next matching row, and it returns true if there was a row to advance to, or false once the result set is exhausted -- which is the only reason the while-loop shape works correctly as both the 'move forward' step and the 'are we done' check.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is the single most common block of ServiceNow server-side code, so I write it the same way every time: construct, addQuery (as many as needed, they AND together automatically), query, then while(gr.next()). The addQuery calls only build conditions in memory -- nothing hits the database until query() runs. And next() isn't just a boolean check, it's doing the actual row-advancing work too, which is exactly why you can't skip the while loop and just check getRowCount() if you intend to read the rows.
commonMistakes: Calling `.query()` and then reading fields without ever calling `.next()`, leaving the cursor unpositioned
Assuming multiple `.addQuery()` calls combine with OR instead of AND by default
Thinking `.addQuery()` touches the database immediately instead of just building up conditions in memory
Forgetting the `while` loop structure and using `if (gr.next())` when more than one result is expected
keyPoints: `new GlideRecord('incident')` creates the cursor; `.addQuery()` builds conditions in memory
Multiple `.addQuery()` calls combine with AND by default
`.query()` is the only line that actually sends the conditions to the database
`.next()` advances the cursor and returns true/false in the same call -- the reason `while(gr.next())` works

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Produces correct, runnable GlideRecord query code
Correctly explains AND-by-default combination of `.addQuery()` calls
Correctly explains what `.next()` returns and why the while loop works

questions.title: Write GlideRecord Code to Insert and Update Incident Records
questions.prompt: Write server-side script that (1) creates a brand-new Incident with a short description, and (2) separately queries an existing Incident by number and updates its priority. Explain which GlideRecord methods make each operation actually happen.
questions.modelAnswer: For the insert, `.initialize()` sets up a new, empty in-memory record with the table's default values, field assignments like `grNew.short_description = '...'` set the values I want on that in-memory record, and `.insert()` is the call that actually writes the new row to the database and returns its sys_id. For the update, the pattern is query-then-update: construct a GlideRecord, add a query condition, call `.query()`, call `.next()` to position the cursor on the matching row (returns true only if a match existed), then assign the new field value directly to the GlideRecord object, and finally call `.update()`, which is the line that actually writes the change back to the database. Skipping `.insert()` or `.update()` leaves the change sitting only in the in-memory object -- nothing is ever persisted.
questions.professionalAnswer: Insert and update both follow a predictable shape: build the object, set the fields, then call the one method that actually commits it. For a new record that's initialize() then insert(); for an existing one it's query-then-next()-then-update(). The thing I watch for every time is making sure next() actually returned true before I touch the record -- updating a GlideRecord object that never matched a row just silently does nothing, it doesn't throw an error.
commonMistakes: Forgetting `.initialize()` before setting fields on a brand-new record
Calling `.insert()` or `.update()` without ever verifying the assignment actually happened first
Not checking `.next()`'s return value before updating, which silently no-ops if no record matched
Using `.insert()` on a record meant to be an update, which creates a duplicate instead of modifying the original
keyPoints: `.initialize()` sets up an empty in-memory record with default values before an insert
`.insert()` is the call that actually writes a new row to the database
An update always follows query → `.next()` → field assignment → `.update()`
`.next()` must return true before it's safe to read or modify the record

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Produces correct insert code using `.initialize()` and `.insert()`
Produces correct update code using query/`.next()`/`.update()`
Correctly explains which call actually commits each operation to the database

questions.title: Write a Class-Based Script Include
questions.prompt: Write a class-based Script Include named `IncidentUtils` with an `initialize` constructor that sets a priority threshold, and a method `isHighPriority(gr)` that returns true if the Incident's priority is at or above that threshold. Explain why the trailing `type` property is required, not just a style choice.
questions.modelAnswer: `Class.create()` is a real ServiceNow platform API that returns a constructor function; assigning an object literal to `IncidentUtils.prototype` defines every method the class has in one place, closer to classical OOP than one-property-at-a-time prototype assignment. `initialize` is the constructor -- it runs automatically the instant `new IncidentUtils()` executes, which is why setting `priorityThreshold` there guarantees it's available before any method reads it. The trailing `type: 'IncidentUtils'` property is a required ServiceNow convention, not decoration: it's a string naming the class, matching the variable name exactly, and the platform's internal reflection uses it to correctly identify the class, for example when logging errors. If a developer renames the class everywhere but forgets to update `type` to match, the code still runs, but the mismatch is a real, latent bug -- any logging or internal reflection that relies on `type` will report the wrong class name.
questions.professionalAnswer: Standard shape: Class.create() for the constructor, a prototype object literal listing initialize plus every method, and a trailing type property that has to match the class name exactly. I treat getting that type string right as non-negotiable -- it's cheap to get wrong during a rename and the failure mode isn't a thrown error, it's silently wrong information wherever the platform's internal reflection looks at type, which makes it a nasty one to debug later.
commonMistakes: Omitting the `type` property entirely, or letting it drift out of sync after a rename
Putting default values outside `initialize`, so they're not guaranteed to be set before a method runs
Forgetting the Script Include's `type` property must match its file/record name on the platform, not just the local variable
Confusing `.prototype = {...}` (an object literal replacing the whole prototype) with assigning properties one at a time
keyPoints: `Class.create()` returns a constructor; `.prototype` lists every method including `initialize`
`initialize` is the constructor, runs automatically at `new ClassName()`
`type` must be a string matching the class name exactly -- required by platform reflection, not stylistic
A `type` left out of sync after a rename doesn't crash the code but silently breaks internal reflection

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Produces correct `Class.create()` / `.prototype` structure with `initialize` and the method
Correctly explains `initialize` as the constructor and when it runs
Correctly explains why `type` is required, not optional style

questions.title: Fix an onChange Client Script That Fires on Form Load
questions.prompt: A Client Script below is supposed to warn the user only when they manually change Priority to 1, but it's also firing the warning the instant the form loads on any Incident that already has Priority 1 saved. Fix the script.
questions.modelAnswer: The fix is adding the standard guard at the top of the function: `if (isLoading || isTemplate) { return; }`. The bug happens because `onChange` fires once when the form loads if the field already had a value -- that's a platform behavior, not a mistake in the rest of the logic -- so without the guard, any Incident saved with Priority 1 re-triggers the message purely from opening the form, before the user has touched anything. `isLoading` is true specifically during that initial form-load firing; checking it first and returning early means the real warning logic only runs on an actual user-driven change afterward.
questions.professionalAnswer: Classic missing-guard bug. onChange fires on load whenever the field already has a value, so the fix is always the same two-line guard at the very top: if isLoading or isTemplate, return immediately, before any real logic runs. Everything else in the script is fine -- it's purely about not letting the load-time firing reach the message logic at all.
commonMistakes: Trying to detect 'is this a load' by checking oldValue instead of using `isLoading`
Adding the guard after some logic has already run, instead of as the very first line
Forgetting `isTemplate` also needs guarding, since templates can pre-populate a field the same way a saved value does
Comparing `newValue` with `===` against a number instead of a string, since onChange values always arrive as strings
keyPoints: onChange fires once on form load if the field already has a value -- not a bug, a platform behavior
The fix is an `if (isLoading || isTemplate) { return; }` guard as the very first line
`oldValue` and `newValue` always arrive as strings, even for numeric/choice fields
Skipping the guard is the single most common onChange bug

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly adds the isLoading/isTemplate guard as the fix
Correctly explains why onChange fires on form load without the guard
Keeps the rest of the logic intact and correct

questions.title: Write a GlideAjax Call From a Client Script
questions.prompt: Write the client-side half of a GlideAjax call to a Script Include named `FreezeWindowChecker`, calling its `checkDateRange` method with two date parameters, and showing an info message on the form if the server answers 'true'. Explain why you can't just read the answer on the line right after the call.
questions.modelAnswer: `new GlideAjax('FreezeWindowChecker')` names the Script Include, which must match its `type` property exactly. `sysparm_name` is the reserved parameter telling GlideAjax which public method to run; every other `sysparm_` name becomes a plain argument read on the server with `getParameter()`. `getXMLAnswer()` doesn't return the server's answer directly -- it takes a callback that runs later, once the server actually responds, because the call is asynchronous. That's exactly why I can't read the answer on the next line after calling it: that next line executes immediately, before the network round-trip has even started, so any variable I tried to capture the answer in would still be undefined at that point. Everything that depends on the answer -- the message, any form update -- has to live inside the callback itself.
questions.professionalAnswer: I build it the same way every time: construct GlideAjax with the Script Include name, addParam sysparm_name with the method, addParam for every real argument, then getXMLAnswer with a callback. The reason I can't just read the result on the next line is that getXMLAnswer is asynchronous by design -- the call goes out, the script keeps running immediately, and the server's answer only shows up later when the callback actually fires. Anything that needs that answer has to live inside the callback, full stop, or it'll be acting on a value that hasn't arrived yet.
commonMistakes: Reading the answer on the line immediately after `getXMLAnswer()` instead of inside its callback
Forgetting `sysparm_name` is the one reserved parameter that selects the server method
Mismatching the GlideAjax constructor's Script Include name against the Script Include's actual `type`
Assuming there's a synchronous alternative to `getXMLAnswer()` for getting the answer immediately
keyPoints: `new GlideAjax('ScriptIncludeName')` must match the Script Include's `type` exactly
`sysparm_name` is reserved for selecting which server method to run
`getXMLAnswer()` is asynchronous -- it takes a callback, it does not return the answer directly
Any code depending on the answer must live inside the callback, not on the line after the call

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Produces correct GlideAjax client-script code with addParam and a callback
Correctly explains why `getXMLAnswer()` is asynchronous
Correctly identifies `sysparm_name`'s special role

questions.title: Build a Flow: Notify a Manager When a Priority 1 Incident Is Created
questions.prompt: A Service Desk manager asks: 'When a new Incident comes in marked Priority 1 - Critical, send a notification to the manager of the group it gets assigned to, so they know immediately.' Walk through building this in Flow Designer end to end: the trigger, the action, and what has to happen before it actually runs against real records.

deepDive.heading: Choosing the trigger
deepDive.content: This is a reaction to something happening -- a new Incident arriving -- not a periodic job, so it's a Record trigger, not a Scheduled trigger. Set the table to Incident and the condition to 'Created' rather than 'Updated,' since the request is about catching the Incident the moment it's new, not reacting to every later edit. Then add the narrowing condition: Priority is 1 - Critical. Without that condition, the flow fires on every new Incident regardless of priority; with it, the flow only starts when a brand-new Incident actually matches Priority 1 at creation.

deepDive.heading: Adding the Notify action
deepDive.content: With the trigger built, add the built-in Notify action, which sends a notification through the instance's existing notification infrastructure. Configure the recipient using a data pill from the trigger -- the triggering Incident's Assignment Group, and from there the manager of that group -- a dynamic reference that resolves differently for every Incident, instead of a hardcoded name. Configure the message to reference the Incident's number and short description, so the manager sees exactly which Incident needs attention without opening the record first.

deepDive.heading: Save versus activate
deepDive.content: A newly built flow saves in an inactive state by default -- it will not run against real records yet. Saving preserves the work and allows continued adjustment; activating is the separate, deliberate step that turns the flow on so the trigger engine actually starts watching for matching Incidents. This two-step separation exists on purpose: it lets you build, review, and even demo a flow to a stakeholder before anything fires. Nothing runs until it's consciously activated.

deepDive.heading: Verifying it actually works
deepDive.content: Before calling it done, confirm the trigger's table, condition, and the Notify action's recipient and message are all correct, then activate. From that moment forward, every new Priority 1 Incident triggers a notification to the right manager automatically, with no one watching the queue by hand. If the manager reports nothing arrived, the first thing to check is whether the flow was ever activated at all -- a flow that's only saved, not activated, produces no errors and no notifications, because it was never actually watching.

questions.modelAnswer: See the structured walkthrough above: Record trigger on Incident/Created with a Priority = 1 condition, a Notify action using data pills from the triggering record, and the deliberate save-then-activate sequence.
questions.professionalAnswer: I translate the plain-language request into the exact vocabulary Flow Designer wants: a Record trigger (not Scheduled, since this reacts to a new record existing), narrowed with a condition so it only fires on Priority 1, then a Notify action wired to the trigering record's data instead of a hardcoded name. The detail I never skip is activation -- a flow that's only saved looks finished and produces zero errors, but it's not watching anything yet.
commonMistakes: Choosing a Scheduled trigger instead of a Record trigger for an event-driven request
Forgetting the Priority narrowing condition, so the flow fires on every new Incident
Hardcoding a recipient instead of using a data pill from the triggering record
Assuming a saved flow is already running, without activating it
keyPoints: Record trigger (not Scheduled) for 'when X happens', set to Created with a Priority condition
Notify action configured with data pills from the trigger record, not fixed values
Saving preserves the configuration; activating is the separate step that makes the flow run
A flow that only looks saved, not activated, produces no errors and no results

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly selects a Record trigger with the right table/condition/filter
Correctly configures the Notify action with dynamic data pills
Correctly explains the save-versus-activate distinction

questions.title: Build and Test an Outbound REST Message
questions.prompt: You need to call an external weather API from ServiceNow. Walk through the steps to configure and test a REST Message record before ever calling it from script, and explain why testing it inside the REST Message record first matters.
questions.modelAnswer: A REST Message record holds the endpoint's base URL, and under it one or more HTTP Methods (GET, POST, etc.), each with its own path, headers, and parameters. The build steps: create the REST Message record with the base URL, add an HTTP Method for the specific operation (e.g. GetCurrentConditions, GET), configure any query parameters or headers it needs (an API key header, a city query parameter), and attach an Authentication Profile if the API requires one. Before writing a single line of script that calls it, the record itself has a Test related link that sends a real request using sample parameter values and shows the actual response, status code, and headers back in the UI. Testing here matters because it isolates integration problems from scripting problems: if the test inside the REST Message fails, the issue is the endpoint, auth, or parameters -- nothing to do with GlideRecord or business logic yet. Only once the test succeeds should the next step be writing the RESTMessageV2 script that calls it from a Business Rule or Script Include.
questions.professionalAnswer: Build the REST Message record with the base URL, add the HTTP Method for the specific call, wire up headers/parameters/auth, and then use the built-in Test link before writing any script at all. That order matters because it separates two completely different failure categories -- 'is the external call itself configured right' versus 'is my script calling it correctly' -- and debugging both at once is exactly how people waste an afternoon chasing the wrong problem.
commonMistakes: Writing the calling script before confirming the REST Message itself works via its built-in Test
Putting authentication details directly on the HTTP Method instead of in a proper Authentication Profile
Hardcoding a parameter value that should be a variable substituted at call time
Assuming a successful Test run guarantees the script-side call will also succeed, skipping script-level error handling
keyPoints: A REST Message record holds a base URL; HTTP Methods under it hold the per-operation path/params/headers
The record has a built-in Test link to send a real request before any script exists
Testing in the record first isolates integration configuration problems from scripting problems
Authentication is configured via an Authentication Profile attached to the REST Message or method

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes the REST Message / HTTP Method structure
Correctly describes using the built-in Test before scripting
Explains why testing first isolates the failure category

questions.title: Build a Minimal Scripted REST API Resource
questions.prompt: Write the server-side script for a Scripted REST API resource that accepts a GET request and returns a JSON list of open Incidents assigned to the requesting user's group, including number and short_description for each.
questions.modelAnswer: A Scripted REST Resource's script receives `request` and `response` objects and the body of the `process` function builds whatever data structure the resource should return -- returning a plain JavaScript object (or array) from the function is automatically serialized to JSON by the platform. Here, a standard GlideRecord query (active Incidents, filtered to the calling user's groups) builds up a plain array of objects, each with just the two fields the API contract promises, and the function returns an object wrapping that array. No manual `JSON.stringify()` is needed -- the Scripted REST API framework handles JSON serialization of whatever the script returns.
questions.professionalAnswer: The shape is always the same: a `process(request, response)` function, real GlideRecord logic inside it filtered to whatever the resource is supposed to expose, and a plain JavaScript object or array as the return value -- the framework serializes that to JSON on its own, I don't call JSON.stringify myself. The only judgment call here is keeping the response shape minimal and intentional: only number and short_description, not every field on the Incident table, because a Scripted REST API is a contract with whoever's consuming it.
commonMistakes: Manually calling `JSON.stringify()` on the return value instead of letting the framework serialize it
Returning the raw GlideRecord object instead of building a plain array/object of just the needed fields
Forgetting to scope the query to the requesting user's context (returning every Incident, not just their group's)
Not using `.addActiveQuery()` or its equivalent, returning closed/canceled Incidents unintentionally
keyPoints: A Scripted REST Resource script's `process(request, response)` function builds the response data
Returning a plain object/array lets the platform serialize it to JSON automatically
The response should expose only the intended fields, not the raw GlideRecord object
Standard GlideRecord querying patterns apply the same way inside a Scripted REST API

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Produces a correct, runnable Scripted REST API resource script
Correctly scopes the query (active, assignment group) and field selection
Correctly explains automatic JSON serialization of the return value

questions.title: Choose the Right Variable Type and Where It Should Live
questions.prompt: Three catalog items -- 'New Laptop Request,' 'Software Install,' and 'Conference Room Booking' -- all need a 'Requester's Cost Center' variable. Which ServiceNow variable type should it use, and should it be defined separately on each item, or in a shared Variable Set? Justify both choices.
questions.modelAnswer: Cost Center should be a Reference variable type, pointing at the cost center table, not a Single Line Text field -- a Reference variable guarantees the answer is an actual valid record that downstream approval or billing workflows can act on, while free text would let someone type a cost center that doesn't exist or has a typo no automated process could resolve. It belongs in a shared Variable Set, not redefined separately on each of the three items: the variable is logically identical across all three (same label, same type, same validation), so defining it once in a Variable Set and attaching that set to all three catalog items means a future fix -- a new cost center option, a wording change -- applies everywhere at once. The test that confirms this: if you'd be copying the variable's configuration from item to item by hand, it belongs in a set.
questions.professionalAnswer: Reference variable, pointed at whatever table holds cost centers, not free text -- I want a real, resolvable record coming back, not a string that might not match anything in billing. And it goes in a Variable Set, because the exact same question is being asked on three unrelated items; defining it three times means three places to fix the same bug later. That's the practical signal I use: the moment I'm about to copy a variable's config from one item to another, I stop and put it in a set instead.
commonMistakes: Using Single Line Text for Cost Center instead of a Reference variable, allowing invalid or typo'd values
Defining the same variable separately on all three items instead of using a shared Variable Set
Assuming every variable automatically belongs in a set, even ones genuinely unique to one item
Confusing a one-to-one Variable Set with a multi-row Variable Set for this single-value use case
keyPoints: Reference variable type guarantees a resolvable, valid record rather than free text
A Variable Set groups logically identical variables once, reusable across many catalog items
A shared variable changed once in the set propagates to every item using that set
The practical test: if you're copying a variable's config between items, it belongs in a set

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly selects Reference as the variable type and justifies it
Correctly recommends a shared Variable Set over per-item definitions
Clear justification tied to real maintenance consequences

questions.title: Configure the Right Mix of UI Policy and Data Policy
questions.prompt: A requirement reads: 'Hide the Vendor field unless Category is Software, and separately, require a Vendor value on every Software-category record regardless of how it was created.' Which mechanism handles each half, and why can't one tool do both?
questions.modelAnswer: The hiding half -- 'hide Vendor unless Category is Software' -- is a UI Policy, condition Category = Software, action Visible = true (hidden otherwise), because Visible/hidden behavior can only ever come from a UI Policy; Data Policies never touch visibility at all. The mandatory half -- 'require Vendor on every Software record regardless of how it's created' -- has to be a Data Policy, condition Category = Software, with Vendor set Mandatory, because that rule must hold true no matter how the record was written: a user filling out the form, an API call, or an import. A UI Policy alone can't make that promise since it only operates in the browser and has no reach over a record created by script or integration. In practice, both configurations are built together: the UI Policy for the clean hide/show form experience, and the Data Policy for the actual data-integrity guarantee.
questions.professionalAnswer: Two separate configurations, not one. Hiding is strictly UI Policy territory -- Data Policies have no concept of Visible at all. Making Vendor mandatory 'no matter how the record was written' is strictly Data Policy territory, because that has to be enforced on the server, where it also catches an API insert or an import that a UI Policy would never see. I'd build both: a UI Policy so the form looks right, a Data Policy so the requirement actually holds everywhere, even outside the form.
commonMistakes: Trying to make Vendor mandatory using only a UI Policy, which an API-created record would silently bypass
Assuming a Data Policy can also hide the field, when Visible/hidden is UI-Policy-only
Building only one of the two configurations when the requirement genuinely has two separate halves
Setting the mandatory condition to apply to every record instead of scoping it to Category = Software
keyPoints: Visible/hidden behavior can only come from a UI Policy, never a Data Policy
A mandatory requirement that must hold 'no matter how the record is written' requires a Data Policy
A UI Policy alone cannot guarantee a rule holds for API- or import-created records
Many real requirements need both a UI Policy and a Data Policy configured together

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly assigns the hiding requirement to a UI Policy
Correctly assigns the mandatory requirement to a Data Policy
Correctly explains why neither tool alone can do both halves

lessonLink.label: Review: UI Policy vs. Data Policy: When to Use Each

questions.title: A User Says They Can't See a Field They Used to See
questions.prompt: A user reports that a field on the Incident form they used to be able to see and edit has disappeared. Walk through how you'd troubleshoot an access-denied issue like this, in order.
questions.modelAnswer: First, identify which operation actually failed -- read, write, create, or delete -- since that immediately narrows which family of ACLs to inspect; a field that 'disappeared' usually means a read ACL is blocking it, not a write ACL. Second, check whether a field-level ACL exists for that specific field on Incident, separate from the table-level `incident.read` ACL, since passing the table-level check doesn't guarantee every field is visible. Third, check what recently changed: was a new ACL added or an existing one's role/condition/script modified around the time the user noticed the problem -- since ACLs AND together, a new narrower rule can silently revoke access without touching the rules that used to work. Fourth, confirm the user's actual roles haven't changed (group membership, role inheritance) independent of the ACL itself. Finally, use the platform's own tools -- the Elevated Privilege / Security Debug option an admin can enable shows exactly which ACL blocked a given field or record for a specific user, which turns a guess into a verified answer.
questions.professionalAnswer: I start narrow: which operation failed -- read, write, create, delete -- because that tells me which ACL family to even look at. Then I check for a field-level ACL on that specific field, since table-level access passing doesn't mean every field shows. Then I check what changed recently -- a new ACL added for an unrelated reason is the single most common cause of 'it used to work.' And if I'm still not sure, I turn on Security Debug, which tells me exactly which ACL denied the field or record for that user, instead of me guessing.
commonMistakes: Jumping straight to assuming the user's role was removed, without checking for a new field-level ACL
Not checking what changed recently on the instance around the time the issue started
Confusing a hidden field (UI Policy) with a field actually blocked by the ACL layer
Skipping the platform's own Security Debug / ACL audit tooling and troubleshooting by trial and error instead
keyPoints: Identify the specific operation (read/write/create/delete) that's actually failing first
Check for a field-level ACL in addition to the table-level ACL
Check what changed recently -- a new ACL is a common cause of regressions
Use the platform's Security Debug tooling to get a definitive answer instead of guessing

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies narrowing by operation as the first step
Correctly checks both table-level and field-level ACLs
Correctly considers recent changes and uses real diagnostic tooling

questions.title: Fix a Query Running Inside a Loop
questions.prompt: The script below queries open Incidents per company, but it's running far too many queries for how few companies exist. Identify the performance bug and rewrite it so it runs one query total.
questions.modelAnswer: This is the N+1 query pattern: one query to get the companies, plus one more query *per company* inside the loop -- 500 companies means 501 total queries, and doubling the number of companies doubles the number of queries. The fix is to query `incident` once, outside any per-row loop, and group the results in memory using a plain JavaScript object keyed by company sys_id: `var incidents = new GlideRecord('incident'); incidents.addQuery('active', true); incidents.query(); var counts = {}; while (incidents.next()) { var companyId = incidents.getValue('company'); counts[companyId] = (counts[companyId] || 0) + 1; }`. Now there's exactly one query against `incident`, no matter how many companies exist, and the counting happens entirely in memory.
questions.professionalAnswer: Classic N+1 -- a query inside a loop over another query's results. The fix is always the same shape: pull everything you need in one query outside the loop, then group it in memory with a plain object keyed by whatever you were filtering on. Here that's one pass over active incidents, bucketed by company sys_id, replacing N+1 queries with exactly 1, regardless of how many companies exist.
commonMistakes: Not recognizing the repeated query-per-iteration shape as N+1
Fixing only the symptom (e.g. adding setLimit) instead of pulling the query outside the loop entirely
Grouping in memory with the wrong key (not the company sys_id), silently producing wrong counts
Still using `.getRowCount()` inside the fixed version instead of counting via the single pass
keyPoints: The bug is N+1: one query for N companies, plus one more query per company inside the loop
501 total queries for 500 companies; the query count scales with company count, not with a fixed cost
The fix: one query against `incident` outside the loop, grouped in memory by company
No matter how many companies exist, the fixed version always runs exactly one query

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the N+1 pattern as the bug
Produces a corrected, one-query, in-memory-grouped rewrite
Correctly explains the scaling problem (queries grow with row count)

questions.title: Reading a Profiler Line That Shows '47 Executions'
questions.prompt: Profiling a slow Business Rule transaction, you see a line like `GlideRecord Query: problem [47 executions] -- 2980 ms`. What does that execution count, by itself, tell you about where the query sits in the script -- before you've even opened the code -- and what's the fix?
questions.modelAnswer: An execution count of 47 for one named table in one transaction is the signature of a query sitting inside a loop, not a single query run once. Nobody writes code that intentionally queries `problem` 47 times in one transaction -- that count is a side effect of putting a fresh GlideRecord query inside a `while` loop over something else, most likely 47 active incidents each individually re-querying their linked problem. The fix, before even opening the profiler further, is almost always to dot-walk the reference field already on the outer record instead of opening a new GlideRecord: if `problem_id` is a reference field on `incident`, reading `incGr.problem_id.number` resolves the related problem's field through the reference ServiceNow already has, with zero extra queries, instead of running a brand-new query for every single incident in the loop.
questions.professionalAnswer: The execution count alone tells me the story before I read a line of code: 47 is not a number anyone writes on purpose, it's what happens when a query sits inside a loop that ran 47 times. My first move is checking whether the field being queried for is already sitting on the outer record as a reference field -- almost always it is, and dot-walking it (`incGr.problem_id.number`) replaces all 47 queries with zero extra ones, because the reference is already resolved without a fresh GlideRecord call.
commonMistakes: Assuming a high execution count means the query itself is inefficient, rather than recognizing it as a loop signature
Opening and rewriting the query's conditions instead of checking whether it belongs inside a loop at all
Not checking whether the needed field is already a reference field reachable by dot-walking
Confusing this repeated-small-query signature with the separate 'one query returns too many rows' performance issue
keyPoints: A repeated execution count for one query in one transaction signals the query sits inside a loop
This is the N+1 pattern's profiler signature, distinct from a single slow query
The fix is almost always dot-walking an existing reference field instead of a fresh GlideRecord query per iteration
The count itself (47) tells the story before the code is even opened

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly interprets the execution count as a query-inside-a-loop signature
Correctly proposes dot-walking as the fix
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: Diagnosing a Business Rule That Seems to Run Forever
questions.prompt: An 'after update' Business Rule on Incident calls `current.update()` to set a related field, and users report the Incident form hanging and the record appearing to save multiple times. What's the likely mistake, and how would you fix the rule?
questions.modelAnswer: Calling `current.update()` inside a Business Rule that itself runs on update is a classic recursive-trigger mistake: the `.update()` call writes the record again, which fires the same 'after update' Business Rule a second time, which calls `.update()` again, and so on -- in the best case this is slow and redundant, in the worst case it's a true infinite loop until the platform's recursion guard or a timeout stops it. The fix depends on what the rule is actually trying to do: if it's setting a field on the *same* record that triggered it, that assignment should happen directly on `current` inside a Before Business Rule instead (no second `.update()` needed, since the Before rule's changes are included in the original save), not an After rule calling `.update()` on itself. If the rule genuinely needs to run after the save and update a *different* record, calling `.update()` on that other GlideRecord object is fine -- the mistake specifically is calling `.update()` on `current` itself from within a rule that update already triggered.
questions.professionalAnswer: That's a self-triggering loop: an after-update rule calling current.update() re-fires the same rule, which calls update() again. The real fix is almost always 'you didn't need the second update() at all' -- if the goal is just setting a field on the record that's already being saved, that belongs in a Before rule modifying current directly, since Before changes land in the original save with no extra write. I'd only keep an explicit .update() call in an After rule if it's genuinely updating a different record, not the one that triggered the rule.
commonMistakes: Not recognizing `current.update()` inside an update-triggered rule as a self-triggering loop
Fixing it by adding a condition check instead of removing the unnecessary second update
Moving the logic to Before but still calling `.update()` there (Before rules modify current without needing it)
Assuming the platform always catches infinite recursion instantly, rather than it sometimes running many times before stopping
keyPoints: Calling `current.update()` inside an update-triggered Business Rule re-fires that same rule
This produces a recursive trigger, visible as repeated saves or a hang
If the goal is modifying the same record, do it in a Before rule directly on `current`, with no extra `.update()`
An explicit `.update()` is only appropriate when updating a different record, not the one that triggered the rule

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the recursive-trigger mistake
Correctly proposes moving same-record logic to a Before rule
Clarity of the fix explanation

questions.title: A Flow Isn't Sending Notifications — Where Do You Look?
questions.prompt: A Flow that's supposed to notify a manager on new Priority 1 Incidents appears to have stopped working -- no notifications are arriving. Walk through the specific places you'd check to diagnose this.
questions.modelAnswer: First, confirm the flow is actually active -- a flow that's saved but never activated produces no errors and no output, which looks identical to a silently broken flow from the outside. Second, check the Flow Execution Log for recent runs: if there are no execution records at all for matching Incidents, the trigger itself isn't firing, which points to the trigger's table/condition configuration rather than the actions inside the flow. If there are execution records but they show as failed or stopped partway, open that specific run and look at exactly which step failed -- a common cause is a data pill referencing a field that's since been renamed, removed, or is empty for a specific record (for example, an Incident whose Assignment Group has no manager set). Third, check whether the condition on the trigger has quietly become too narrow or too broad due to an unrelated change elsewhere (a choice list value renamed, for instance) so matching records no longer actually match. The Flow Execution Log is the single most useful tool here because it shows exactly which step a run stopped at, instead of forcing a guess.
questions.professionalAnswer: First thing, always: is it even active? A flow that looks finished but was never activated fails completely silently -- no error, no log entry, nothing. Past that, I go straight to the Flow Execution Log. No runs at all means the trigger isn't firing -- check the trigger's table and condition. Runs that exist but failed partway tell me exactly which step broke, which is usually a data pill pointing at something that's empty or renamed for a specific record, like an assignment group with no manager configured.
commonMistakes: Assuming the flow is active without verifying it, when 'saved but not activated' looks identical to 'broken' from outside
Troubleshooting by re-reading the flow's configuration instead of checking the Flow Execution Log first
Not checking whether a referenced field (like a data pill) is empty or renamed for specific records
Assuming a trigger condition that worked before can't have quietly stopped matching due to an unrelated change
keyPoints: Confirm the flow is actually active, since inactive flows fail with no visible error
Check the Flow Execution Log for whether runs exist at all, and where they fail if they do
No runs at all points to the trigger not firing; failed runs point to a specific broken step
A common root cause is a data pill referencing an empty or renamed field for specific records

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly checks flow activation status first
Correctly uses the Flow Execution Log to localize the failure
Identifies realistic root causes (data pill, trigger condition)
